children: By Amanda Lee and Fabiana Negrin Ochoa
BANGKOK--The energy shock has stoked expectations of interest-rate hikes to tame inflation, but Thailand's central bank has room to wait, a top official says.

"We can afford to be at our current stance, which is accommodative," the Bank of Thailand's Piti Disyatat said on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Group meetings in Bangkok.
It's a luxury not all policymakers have as war in the Middle East disrupts oil and gas flows, sending prices soaring.

The Bank of Thailand is in the shrinking camp of central banks that has yet to tighten policy settings during a year where others--including the Federal Reserve--have raised rates to combat inflation.
An energy importer that gets about half of its oil from the Middle East, Thailand has felt the heat, but not to the extent one might expect.

"Our economy [has] held up quite well," said Piti, deputy governor for monetary stability at the BOT. "The low starting point [of inflation] was definitely to our advantage going into this oil price shock."
Inflation in the Southeast Asian economy has accelerated, printing at 2.8% on the year last month. In February, before the war broke out, Thailand was still in deflation territory.
"It's elevated, but it's not high," Piti said, adding that annual inflation is set to come in on target.
When the BOT updates projections in a couple of weeks, it will substantially lower its average inflation forecast for 2026 from the 2.8% predicted in June.
"And we expect it to come down early next year as well," said Piti.

The revision reflects a change in the BOT's predictions for another inflationary risk: El Nino, the weather phenomenon that causes extreme rainfall and drought. The bank has pushed out its timeline for the dry season, meaning it now expects to see food prices go up next year instead.
Near term, there is no reason for the BOT to break its streak of not raising rates since September 2023.
There's nothing right now that warrants an immediate adjustment to policy settings, "but it's conditional," Piti said.

As long as macroeconomic conditions remain stable, the central bank can maintain its supportive stance. Things look steady on that front, Piti said: Thailand's banking sector is quite strong, so financial stability is not a concern, while exchange-rate volatility is roughly contained.
The lack of pressure to tighten is welcome news considering that Thailand's economic growth remains below potential despite a tailwind from the global artificial-intelligence investment boom.
Exports and investment are doing well because of AI, but consumption is weaker, Piti said.
Echoing concerns raised by the IMF, he noted the "extremely high concentration" of AI benefits.
Demand for AI-related goods has driven better-than-expected export growth this year, but the windfall isn't widespread.
"If you look at, say, the top 1% of exporters in that category, around 80 firms make up 82% of the share of the total value of those exports," Piti said.
The oil shock, on the other hand, hits everybody, the deputy governor said.
The energy crisis may not yet be manifesting as an inflationary threat in Thailand, but it is showing up in consumption numbers.
"The purchasing power erosion from [higher] oil prices is visible," Piti said.
Unlike with inflation, the Thai economy entered the oil shock in an unfavorable position on the demand front.
Still, the BOT doesn't see a case for cutting rates.
At 1%, the Thai policy rate is historically low.
"It would take quite an extraordinary shock to push us lower," Piti said. The central bank also needs to have buffers, "and at this rate, we have some left."
All told, the BOT seems set to hold at its next rate meeting on Oct. 28.
It gathers against a daunting backdrop of external risks, continuing to monitor oil market developments, bond yield volatility and the risk of an AI investment pullback.
But Piti said the BOT's experience with shocks like wars and tariffs has taught it to avoid knee-jerk reactions.
"You just have to look through the noise."
